question: What are the most important ‘proportionality’ criteria within the meaning of Article 12(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/9441 that Latvia must abide by, and does the Commission have examples of good practice from other Member States?

Does ‘direct economic loss’ as referred to in Article 12(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/944, denote not only expenses relating to the conclusion of the contract (such as risk insurance) but also the profit that the supplier will forego in the future?

At first glance, an interpretation of the concept of direct economic loss that would require users to pay the profit foregone by a supplier for the entire duration of the contract would render switching suppliers economically meaningless and would conflict with the objective set out in Article 1 of Directive (EU) 2019/944, namely, to create truly integrated competitive, consumer-centred, flexible, fair and transparent electricity markets.
Has an infringement procedure been brought against Latvia for the improper transposition of Article 12 of Directive (EU) 2019/944 into national legislation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.11.2025) ‘Proportionality’ is always assessed on a case-by-case basis. In this case, it should be assessed in light of the service provided to the customer and cost incurred by the supplier. National regulatory bodies or the Commission's own reports or communications are a good resource to explore specific national examples.

In the Commission’s view, ‘Direct economic loss’ should entail only costs incurred by suppliers, directly related to customers' termination of contracts, including costs of any bundle investments or services already provided (e.g. administrative or acquisition costs). Any future possible profit loss should not be included as this cannot be directly related to the switching of individual customers.

The burden of proof is on the supplier, and the national regulatory authority should monitor the permissibility of such fees. The Commission regularly publishes information1 on its enforcement activities, press releases2 on Member State’s compliance with EU law, and information about Commission decisions3 on infringements.
The Commission currently assesses transposition of the Electricity Directive4 in all Member States, including Latvia, but does not comment on the contents of individual ongoing infringements.
